q: Which row correctly describes a catalysed and an uncatalysed reaction pathway for the same reaction?
options: lower ΔH with a catalyst | same Ea
higher ΔH with a catalyst | lower Ea with a catalyst
same ΔH | higher Ea with a catalyst
same ΔH | lower Ea with a catalyst
explain: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway of lower activation energy without changing the overall energy change.

q: A student adds a sample of an unknown solid to dilute acid and observes that the temperature of the mixture rises. Which row is correct?
options: endothermic | energy absorbed from the surroundings
exothermic | energy absorbed from the surroundings
endothermic | energy released to the surroundings
exothermic | energy released to the surroundings
explain: A temperature rise means that thermal energy is given out, which defines an exothermic reaction.

q: Many exothermic reactions, such as burning methane, do not start until a flame or spark is applied. What is the reason?
options: ΔH only becomes negative after the reaction is started.
The colliding particles must first be given enough energy to overcome the activation energy.
The reaction is actually endothermic until it has started.
The activation energy is released as soon as the reactants are mixed.
explain: Even exothermic reactions have an energy barrier; the spark supplies the energy for the first collisions to react.

q: Use the bond energies (H–H 436 kJ/mol, Cl–Cl 243 kJ/mol, H–Cl 432 kJ/mol) to calculate ΔH for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g).
options: +1543 kJ/mol
−864 kJ/mol
+185 kJ/mol
−185 kJ/mol
explain: Bonds broken: 436 + 243 = 679. Bonds made: 2 × 432 = 864. ΔH = 679 − 864 = −185 kJ/mol.

q: Which statement about endothermic reactions is correct?
options: The surroundings gain thermal energy and the products have more chemical energy than the reactants.
The surroundings gain thermal energy and the products have less chemical energy than the reactants.
The surroundings lose thermal energy and the products have more chemical energy than the reactants.
The surroundings lose thermal energy and the products have less chemical energy than the reactants.
explain: Energy taken from the surroundings ends up stored in the products.

q: Which statement about activation energy is correct?
options: Activation energy is equal to the energy released in an exothermic reaction.
Exothermic and endothermic reactions can both have a high or a low activation energy.
A reaction with a negative ΔH has no activation energy.
Exothermic reactions always have a lower activation energy than endothermic reactions.
explain: Ea depends on the height of the peak above the reactants and is independent of the sign of ΔH.

q: Which equation represents an endothermic reaction?
options: 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s)
CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g)
CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)
NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)
explain: Thermal decomposition reactions are endothermic; combustion and neutralisation are exothermic.

q: Which row correctly describes an exothermic reaction?
columns: Energy of products compared with reactants
options: thermal energy given out to surroundings | temperature of surroundings increases | energy of products higher than reactants
thermal energy given out to surroundings | temperature of surroundings increases | energy of products lower than reactants
thermal energy given out to surroundings | temperature of surroundings decreases | energy of products lower than reactants
thermal energy taken in from surroundings | temperature of surroundings increases | energy of products lower than reactants
explain: In an exothermic reaction energy is released, the surroundings warm and the products end up lower in energy.

q: Use the bond energies (C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O 805, O–H 464, all in kJ/mol) to calculate ΔH for CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g).
options: −818 kJ/mol
−2648 kJ/mol
+818 kJ/mol
−3466 kJ/mol

q: On a reaction pathway diagram, which part represents the activation energy?
options: the energy of the reactants measured from the horizontal axis
the energy difference between the products and the highest point of the curve
the energy difference between the reactants and the highest point of the curve
the energy difference between the reactants and the products
explain: Ea is the energy barrier that must be climbed from the reactants level up to the peak.

q: A self-heating food can contains calcium oxide and water kept apart. When the two are mixed the can gets hot. What type of reaction takes place?
options: neither exothermic nor endothermic
endothermic
exothermic
both exothermic and endothermic at the same time
explain: The mixture gets hotter because thermal energy is released, so the reaction is exothermic.

q: Use the bond energies (N≡N 945, H–H 436, N–H 391, all in kJ/mol) to calculate ΔH for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g).
options: +93 kJ/mol
−93 kJ/mol
−2346 kJ/mol
+2253 kJ/mol

q: On a reaction pathway diagram, a downward arrow drawn from the reactants level to the lower products level represents what?
options: the thermal energy released to the surroundings in the reaction
the thermal energy absorbed from the surroundings in the reaction
the time taken for the reaction
the temperature of the reaction mixture
explain: The size of the drop in energy is the amount of energy transferred to the surroundings.

q: Which is a use of an endothermic process?
options: using a self-heating can to warm soup
using an instant cold pack on a sprained ankle
using a hand warmer in winter
burning charcoal on a barbecue
explain: A cold pack works because dissolving the solid takes in thermal energy.

q: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to sodium hydroxide solution. The temperature rises from 20.0 °C to 26.5 °C. What is the temperature change and the type of reaction?
options: a decrease of 6.5 °C; endothermic
a decrease of 6.5 °C; exothermic
an increase of 6.5 °C; exothermic
an increase of 6.5 °C; endothermic
explain: 26.5 − 20.0 = 6.5 °C rise, showing that energy is given out, so the reaction is exothermic.

q: The temperature of the surroundings rises during a reaction. Which statement about the energy of the substances must be correct?
options: The products contain more energy than the reactants.
Thermal energy is transferred from the surroundings to the products as chemical energy.
No energy is transferred between the reactants and the surroundings.
Chemical energy is transferred from the reactants to the surroundings as thermal energy.
explain: Surroundings gain energy only if the reacting chemicals have lost it.

q: Zinc powder is added to copper(II) sulfate solution and the temperature rises by 8 °C. Which statement is correct?
options: The reaction takes in thermal energy from the solution.
The reaction is exothermic.
The reaction is endothermic.
The solution loses energy to the zinc.
explain: A rise in temperature of the solution means thermal energy has been transferred to it, so the reaction is exothermic.

q: Which row correctly describes bond breaking and bond making?
options: bond breaking: endothermic | bond making: exothermic
bond breaking: exothermic | bond making: endothermic
bond breaking: exothermic | bond making: exothermic
bond breaking: endothermic | bond making: endothermic
explain: Energy must be put in to break bonds, and energy is released when new bonds form.

q: The equation for the combustion of methane is CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l). Which statement is correct?
options: Thermal energy is taken in from the surroundings during the reaction.
The temperature of the surroundings decreases.
The reaction is endothermic.
Thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings during the reaction.
explain: All combustion reactions are exothermic.

q: Use the bond energies (H–H 436, Br–Br 193, H–Br 366, all in kJ/mol) to calculate ΔH for H₂(g) + Br₂(g) → 2HBr(g).
options: −1361 kJ/mol
+103 kJ/mol
−103 kJ/mol
−732 kJ/mol

q: The enthalpy change for the reaction H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g) is −185 kJ/mol. What is the enthalpy change for 2H₂(g) + 2Cl₂(g) → 4HCl(g)?
options: +370 kJ/mol
−92.5 kJ/mol
−370 kJ/mol
−185 kJ/mol
explain: The equation has been doubled, so twice as much energy is released: 2 × (−185) = −370 kJ/mol.

q: A reaction pathway diagram shows reactants at 150 kJ/mol, a peak at 400 kJ/mol and products at 90 kJ/mol. What are ΔH and Ea?
options: ΔH = +60 kJ/mol | Ea = +250 kJ/mol
ΔH = −250 kJ/mol | Ea = +60 kJ/mol
ΔH = −60 kJ/mol | Ea = +310 kJ/mol
ΔH = −60 kJ/mol | Ea = +250 kJ/mol

q: Use the bond energies (C=C 614, H–H 436, C–C 347, C–H 413, all in kJ/mol) to calculate ΔH for C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g).
options: −1050 kJ/mol
+123 kJ/mol
−123 kJ/mol
−1173 kJ/mol

q: Which statement about the surroundings is correct?
options: In both endothermic and exothermic reactions the surroundings lose thermal energy.
In an endothermic reaction the surroundings lose thermal energy; in an exothermic reaction they gain it.
In both endothermic and exothermic reactions the surroundings gain thermal energy.
In an endothermic reaction the surroundings gain thermal energy; in an exothermic reaction they lose it.
explain: Energy is transferred from the reaction to the surroundings in exothermic changes, and the other way round in endothermic ones.

q: Which process releases thermal energy to its surroundings?
options: the dissolving of ammonium chloride in water
the thermal decomposition of copper(II) carbonate
respiration
photosynthesis
explain: Respiration releases energy to the organism and its surroundings; the other processes absorb energy.

q: A student holds a test tube while two solutions react in it. The tube feels cold. What is the explanation?
options: The reaction is endothermic and takes in thermal energy from the student's hand.
The reaction is exothermic and takes in thermal energy from the student's hand.
The reaction is endothermic and gives out thermal energy to the student's hand.
The reaction is exothermic and gives out thermal energy to the student's hand.
explain: Cold means energy is leaving the surroundings and entering the reaction, so it is endothermic.

q: Which statement about reactions is correct?
options: Reactions that produce a gas are always exothermic.
All reactions that need heating to start are endothermic.
Reactions in which the temperature of the surroundings rises are endothermic.
Reactions in which the temperature of the surroundings rises are exothermic.
explain: The sign of the temperature change of the surroundings tells you the type of reaction; needing a start-up does not.

q: Which row correctly links the sign of ΔH to the type of reaction and the effect on the surroundings?
options: ΔH negative | exothermic | surroundings get warmer
ΔH positive | exothermic | surroundings get colder
ΔH positive | endothermic | surroundings get warmer
ΔH negative | endothermic | surroundings get warmer
explain: Negative ΔH = energy released = exothermic = surroundings warm up.

q: Which statement describes an endothermic reaction?
options: It takes in thermal energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises.
It transfers thermal energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises.
It takes in thermal energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
It transfers thermal energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
explain: An endothermic reaction absorbs thermal energy from its surroundings, which therefore get colder.

q: Which reaction would make a thermometer in the mixture show the largest fall in temperature?
options: an exothermic reaction giving out a small amount of thermal energy
an endothermic reaction taking in a large amount of thermal energy
a reaction that gives out and takes in no thermal energy
an exothermic reaction giving out a large amount of thermal energy
explain: The more energy an endothermic reaction absorbs, the bigger the temperature drop.
